title: Relative Strengths of Acids and Bases
short: Relative Strengths of Acids and Bases
lead: Some acids and bases ionize almost completely in water and others only slightly. This section measures that strength with ionization constants and percent ionization, compares the strengths of conjugate partners, works through equilibrium calculations for solutions of weak acids and bases, and looks at how the structure of a molecule sets its acid strength.
objectives: Assess the relative strengths of acids and bases according to their ionization constants
Rationalize trends in acid–base strength in relation to molecular structure
Carry out equilibrium calculations for weak acid–base systems
summary_html: The relative strengths of acids and bases are reflected in the magnitudes of their ionization constants; the stronger the acid or base, the larger its ionization constant. A reciprocal relation exists between the strengths of a conjugate acid-base pair: the stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base. Water exerts a leveling effect on dissolved acids or bases, reacting completely to generate its characteristic hydronium and hydroxide ions (the strongest acid and base that may exist in water). The strengths of the binary acids increase from left to right across a period of the periodic table (CH4 < NH3 < H2O < HF), and they increase down a group (HF < HCl < HBr < HI). The strengths of oxyacids that contain the same central element increase as the oxidation number of the element increases (H2SO3 < H2SO4). The strengths of oxyacids also increase as the electronegativity of the central element increases [H2SeO4 < H2SO4].
notes: The Link to Learning pointing to a simulation of strong and weak acids and bases at the molecular level is left out, and the Sim after Example 14.7 takes its place. The book’s “wheres”, “much lesser than”, CH<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> for acetate ion in the order of base strengths, the Check Your Learning of Example 14.11 ending in a period, and the empty Change cell for formic acid in the ICE table of Example 14.12 are kept as printed.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the percent ionization of a 0.10-M solution of acetic acid with a pH of 2.89.

answer.hint: Convert the pH to [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] = 10<sup>−pH</sup>, divide by the initial concentration of the acid, and multiply by 100.
answer.solution: 1.3% ionized

exercises.prompt: Determine the relative acid strengths of ${\text{NH}}_{4}{}^{\text{+}}$ and HCN by comparing their ionization constants. The ionization constant of HCN is given in Appendix H as 4.9 × 10<sup>−10</sup>. The ionization constant of ${\text{NH}}_{4}{}^{\text{+}}$ is not listed, but the ionization constant of its conjugate base, NH<sub>3</sub>, is listed as 1.8 × 10<sup>−5</sup>.

answer.hint: Find Ka for NH4+ as Kw/Kb of NH3, then compare it with Ka for HCN.
answer.solution: ${\text{NH}}_{4}{}^{\text{+}}$ is the slightly stronger acid (Ka for ${\text{NH}}_{4}{}^{\text{+}}$ = 5.6 × 10−10).

exercises.prompt:
The ${\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{\text{-}}$ ion, weak acid used in some household cleansers:
${\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{\text{-}}(aq)+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(l)\;\rightleftharpoons \;{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{\text{+}}(aq)+{\text{SO}}_{4}{}^{2-}(aq)$
What is the acid ionization constant for this weak acid if an equilibrium mixture has the following composition: $[{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{\text{+}}]$ = 0.027 M; $[{\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{\text{-}}]=0.29\;M;$ and $[{\text{SO}}_{4}{}^{2-}]=0.13\;M?$

answer.hint: Substitute the three equilibrium concentrations into Ka = [H3O+][SO42−]/[HSO4−].
answer.solution: Ka for ${\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{\text{-}}$ = 1.2 × 10−2

exercises.prompt:
What is the equilibrium constant for the ionization of the ${\text{HPO}}_{4}{}^{2-}$ ion, a weak base
${\text{HPO}}_{4}{}^{2-}(aq)+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(l)\;\rightleftharpoons \;{\text{H}}_{2}{\text{PO}}_{4}{}^{\text{-}}(aq)+{\text{OH}}^{\text{-}}(aq)$
if the composition of an equilibrium mixture is as follows: [OH−] = 1.3 × 10−6 M; $[{\text{H}}_{2}{\text{PO}}_{4}{}^{\text{-}}]=0.042\;M;$ and $[{\text{HPO}}_{4}{}^{2-}]=0.341\;M?$
The pH of a solution of household ammonia, a 0.950-M solution of NH3, is 11.612. What is Kb for NH3.

answer.hint: The pOH, 14.00 − pH, gives [OH−] = [NH4+]; an ICE table from 0.950 M gives [NH3] at equilibrium.
answer.solution: Kb = 1.8 × 10−5

exercises.prompt:
Only a small fraction of a weak acid ionizes in aqueous solution. What is the percent ionization of a 0.100-M solution of acetic acid, CH3CO2H?
${\text{CH}}_{3}{\text{CO}}_{2}\text{H}(aq)+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(l)\;\rightleftharpoons \;{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{\text{+}}(aq)+{\text{CH}}_{3}{\text{CO}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}}(aq)\hspace{5em}{K}_{\text{a}}=1.8\;\times \;{10}^{-5}$

answer.hint: Solve x2/(0.100 − x) = 1.8 × 10−5 for x = [H3O+], then divide by 0.100 and multiply by 100.
answer.solution: percent ionization = 1.3%

exercises.prompt: Calculate the hydroxide ion concentration and the percent ionization of a 0.0325-M solution of ammonia, a weak base with a Kb of 1.76 × 10−5.

Calculate the pH in a 0.010-M solution of caffeine, a weak base:
${\text{C}}_{8}{\text{H}}_{10}{\text{N}}_{4}{\text{O}}_{2}(aq)+{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}(l)\;\rightleftharpoons \;{\text{C}}_{8}{\text{H}}_{10}{\text{N}}_{4}{\text{O}}_{2}{\text{H}}^{\text{+}}(aq)+{\text{OH}}^{\text{-}}(aq)\hspace{5em}{K}_{\text{b}}=2.5\;\times \;{10}^{-4}$

answer.hint: Let x = [OH−] and solve x2/(0.010 − x) = 2.5 × 10−4; x is not small against 0.010, so use the quadratic formula. Then pH = 14.00 − pOH.

exercises.prompt:
Use this list of important industrial compounds (and Figure 14.8) to answer the following questions regarding: Ca(OH)2, CH3CO2H, HCl, H2CO3, HF, HNO2, HNO3, H3PO4, H2SO4, NH3, NaOH, Na2CO3.
(a) Identify the strong Brønsted-Lowry acids and strong Brønsted-Lowry bases.
(b) Identify the compounds that can behave as Brønsted-Lowry acids with strengths lying between those of H3O+ and H2O.
(c) Identify the compounds that can behave as Brønsted-Lowry bases with strengths lying between those of H2O and OH−.

answer.solution: Suggested approach: find each compound in Figure 14.8, or see that it releases hydroxide ion, as NaOH and Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> do. Acids listed above hydronium ion and bases listed below hydroxide ion ionize completely in water; acids between hydronium ion and water, and bases between water and hydroxide ion, ionize only partly. A compound may appear in both columns.

exercises.prompt: The odor of vinegar is due to the presence of acetic acid, CH3CO2H, a weak acid. List, in order of descending concentration, all of the ionic and molecular species present in a 1-M aqueous solution of this acid.

answer.solution: [H<sub>2</sub>O] > [CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H] > $[{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{\text{+}}]$ ≈ $[{\text{CH}}_{3}{\text{CO}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}}]$ > [OH<sup>−</sup>]

exercises.prompt: Household ammonia is a solution of the weak base NH3 in water. List, in order of descending concentration, all of the ionic and molecular species present in a 1-M aqueous solution of this base.

answer.solution: Suggested approach: follow the answer for acetic acid in the exercise before this one. Write the ionization of NH3 with water, remember that a weak base ionizes only slightly, and compare the concentration of the solvent with that of every solute; place hydronium ion using Kw = [H3O+][OH−].

exercises.prompt: Explain why the ionization constant, Ka, for H2SO4 is larger than the ionization constant for H2SO3.

answer.solution: The oxidation state of the sulfur in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is greater than the oxidation state of the sulfur in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub>.

exercises.prompt: Explain why the ionization constant, Ka, for HI is larger than the ionization constant for HF.

answer.solution: Suggested approach: HF and HI are binary acids of the same group. Compare the strengths of the H–F and H–I bonds, as the text does for group 17, and say which bond breaks more readily when the acid ionizes in water.

exercises.prompt: Gastric juice, the digestive fluid produced in the stomach, contains hydrochloric acid, HCl. Milk of Magnesia, a suspension of solid Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> in an aqueous medium, is sometimes used to neutralize excess stomach acid. Write a complete balanced equation for the neutralization reaction, and identify the conjugate acid-base pairs.

answer.solution: $\begin{array}{lllllll}\text{Mg}{(\text{OH})}_{2}(s)+ & \text{2HCl}(aq) & \;\longrightarrow \; & {\text{Mg}}^{2+}(aq)+ & 2{\text{Cl}}^{\text{-}}(aq)+\; & {\text{2H}}_{2}\text{O}(l) \\ \text{BB} & \text{BA} & & & \text{CB} & \text{CA} & \end{array}$

exercises.prompt: Nitric acid reacts with insoluble copper(II) oxide to form soluble copper(II) nitrate, Cu(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, a compound that has been used to prevent the growth of algae in swimming pools. Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction of an aqueous solution of HNO<sub>3</sub> with CuO.

answer.solution: Suggested approach: copper(II) oxide acts as a base toward the strong acid. Write copper(II) nitrate and water as the products, then balance the copper, nitrogen, oxygen and hydrogen atoms.

exercises.prompt: What is the ionization constant at 25 °C for the weak acid ${\text{CH}}_{3}{\text{NH}}_{3}{}^{\text{+}},$ the conjugate acid of the weak base CH3NH2, Kb = 4.4 × 10−4.

Which base, CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> or (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>NH, is the stronger base? Which conjugate acid, ${({\text{CH}}_{3})}_{2}{\text{NH}}_{2}{}^{\text{+}}$ or ${\text{CH}}_{3}{\text{NH}}_{3}{}^{\text{+}}$, is the stronger acid?

answer.solution: The stronger base or stronger acid is the one with the larger Kb or Ka, respectively. In these two examples, they are (CH3)2NH and ${\text{CH}}_{3}{\text{NH}}_{3}{}^{\text{+}}.$

exercises.prompt: Which is the stronger acid, ${\text{NH}}_{4}{}^{\text{+}}$ or HBrO?

answer.solution: Suggested approach: look up Ka for HBrO in Appendix H and find Ka for NH4+ from Kw and the Kb of NH3 in Appendix I, as the Check Your Learning of Example 14.8 does; the larger constant belongs to the stronger acid.

exercises.prompt: Which is the stronger base, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>N or ${\text{H}}_{2}{\text{BO}}_{3}{}^{\text{-}}?$

answer.solution: triethylamine

exercises.prompt:
Predict which acid in each of the following pairs is the stronger and explain your reasoning for each.
(a) H2O or HF
(b) B(OH)3 or Al(OH)3
(c) ${\text{HSO}}_{3}{}^{\text{-}}$ or ${\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{\text{-}}$
(d) NH3 or H2S
(e) H2O or H2Te

answer.solution: Suggested approach: decide for each pair whether the two are binary acids, ranked across a row by electronegativity and down a group by bond strength, or hydroxy compounds and oxyacids, ranked by the electronegativity and the oxidation number of the central atom; then apply that trend.

exercises.prompt:
Predict which compound in each of the following pairs of compounds is more acidic and explain your reasoning for each.
(a) ${\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{\text{-}}$ or ${\text{HSeO}}_{4}{}^{\text{-}}$
(b) NH3 or H2O
(c) PH3 or HI
(d) NH3 or PH3
(e) H2S or HBr

answer.solution: (a) ${\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{\text{-}};$ higher electronegativity of the central ion. (b) H2O; NH3 is a base and water is neutral, or decide on the basis of Ka values. (c) HI; PH3 is weaker than HCl; HCl is weaker than HI. Thus, PH3 is weaker than HI. (d) PH3; in binary compounds of hydrogen with nonmetals, the acidity increases for the element lower in a group. (e) HBr; in a period, the acidity increases from left to right; in a group, it increases from top to bottom. Br is to the left and below S, so HBr is the stronger acid.

exercises.prompt:
Rank the compounds in each of the following groups in order of increasing acidity or basicity, as indicated, and explain the order you assign.
(a) acidity: HCl, HBr, HI
(b) basicity: H2O, OH−, H−, Cl−
(c) basicity: Mg(OH)2, Si(OH)4, ClO3(OH) (Hint: Formula could also be written as HClO4.)
(d) acidity: HF, H2O, NH3, CH4

answer.solution: Suggested approach: parts (a) and (d) are binary acids, ranked by the trends down a group and across a row; for (b) use the base column of Figure 14.8 and the reciprocal strengths of conjugate partners; for (c) compare the electronegativities of Mg, Si and Cl as the central atoms of hydroxy compounds.

exercises.prompt:
Rank the compounds in each of the following groups in order of increasing acidity or basicity, as indicated, and explain the order you assign.
(a) acidity: NaHSO3, NaHSeO3, NaHSO4
(b) basicity: ${\text{BrO}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}},$ ${\text{ClO}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}},$ ${\text{IO}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}}$
(c) acidity: HOCl, HOBr, HOI
(d) acidity: HOCl, HOClO, HOClO2, HOClO3
(e) basicity: ${\text{NH}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}},$ HS−, HTe−, ${\text{PH}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}}$
(f) basicity: BrO−, ${\text{BrO}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}},$ ${\text{BrO}}_{3}{}^{\text{-}},$ ${\text{BrO}}_{4}{}^{\text{-}}$

answer.solution: (a) NaHSeO<sub>3</sub> < NaHSO<sub>3</sub> < NaHSO<sub>4</sub>; in polyoxy acids, the more electronegative central element—S, in this case—forms the stronger acid. The larger number of oxygen atoms on the central atom (giving it a higher oxidation state) also creates a greater release of hydrogen atoms, resulting in a stronger acid. As a salt, the acidity increases in the same manner. (b) ${\text{ClO}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}}<{\text{BrO}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}}<{\text{IO}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}};$ the basicity of the anions in a series of acids will be the opposite of the acidity in their oxyacids. The acidity increases as the electronegativity of the central atom increases. Cl is more electronegative than Br, and I is the least electronegative of the three. (c) HOI < HOBr < HOCl; in a series of the same form of oxyacids, the acidity increases as the electronegativity of the central atom increases. Cl is more electronegative than Br, and I is the least electronegative of the three. (d) HOCl < HOClO < HOClO<sub>2</sub> < HOClO<sub>3</sub>; in a series of oxyacids of the same central element, the acidity increases as the number of oxygen atoms increases (or as the oxidation state of the central atom increases). (e) ${\text{HTe}}^{\text{-}}<{\text{HS}}^{\text{-}}\ll \;{\text{PH}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}}<{\text{NH}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}};$ ${\text{PH}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}}$ and ${\text{NH}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}}$ are anions of weak bases, so they act as strong bases toward H<sup>+</sup>. ${\text{HTe}}^{\text{-}}$ and HS<sup>−</sup> are anions of weak acids, so they have less basic character. In a periodic group, the more electronegative element has the more basic anion. (f) ${\text{BrO}}_{4}{}^{\text{-}}<{\text{BrO}}_{3}{}^{\text{-}}<{\text{BrO}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}}<{\text{BrO}}^{\text{-}};$ with a larger number of oxygen atoms (that is, as the oxidation state of the central ion increases), the corresponding acid becomes more acidic and the anion consequently less basic.

exercises.prompt: Both HF and HCN ionize in water to a limited extent. Which of the conjugate bases, F<sup>−</sup> or CN<sup>−</sup>, is the stronger base?

answer.solution: Suggested approach: look up Ka for HF and for HCN in Appendix H. Since Kb = Kw/Ka, the conjugate base of the weaker acid is the stronger base.

exercises.prompt: The active ingredient formed by aspirin in the body is salicylic acid, C6H4OH(CO2H). The carboxyl group (−CO2H) acts as a weak acid. The phenol group (an OH group bonded to an aromatic ring) also acts as an acid but a much weaker acid. List, in order of descending concentration, all of the ionic and molecular species present in a 0.001-M aqueous solution of C6H4OH(CO2H).
Are the concentrations of hydronium ion and hydroxide ion in a solution of an acid or a base in water directly proportional or inversely proportional? Explain your answer.

answer.solution: Suggested approach: every aqueous solution obeys Kw = [H3O+][OH−] at a given temperature. Ask what must happen to one of the two concentrations when the other is made ten times larger while their product stays fixed.

exercises.prompt: What two common assumptions can simplify calculation of equilibrium concentrations in a solution of a weak acid or base?

answer.solution: 1. Assume that the change in initial concentration of the acid as the equilibrium is established can be neglected, so this concentration can be assumed constant and equal to the initial value of the total acid concentration. 2. Assume we can neglect the contribution of water to the equilibrium concentration of H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>.

exercises.prompt: Which of the following will increase the percent of NH<sub>3</sub> that is converted to the ammonium ion in water?

answer.hint: Write NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>−</sup> and ask which addition removes a product, shifting the equilibrium to the right.
answer.solution: (b) The addition of HCl

exercises.prompt:
Which of the following will increase the percentage of HF that is converted to the fluoride ion in water?
(a) addition of NaOH
(b) addition of HCl
(c) addition of NaF

answer.solution: Suggested approach: write HF + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> + F<sup>−</sup>. For each addition, decide which species of the equation it adds, or which its ions react with, and which way Le Châtelier’s principle then shifts the equilibrium; compare with the keyed answer for ammonia in the exercise before this one.

exercises.prompt:
What is the effect on the concentrations of ${\text{NO}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}},$ HNO2, and OH− when the following are added to a solution of KNO2 in water:
(a) HCl
(b) HNO2
(c) NaOH
(d) NaCl
(e) KNO2

answer.solution: (a) Adding HCl will add H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> ions, which will then react with the OH<sup>−</sup> ions, lowering their concentration. The equilibrium will shift to the right, increasing the concentration of HNO<sub>2</sub>, and decreasing the concentration of ${\text{NO}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}}$ ions. (b) Adding HNO<sub>2</sub> increases the concentration of HNO<sub>2</sub> and shifts the equilibrium to the left, increasing the concentration of ${\text{NO}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}}$ ions and decreasing the concentration of OH<sup>−</sup> ions. (c) Adding NaOH adds OH<sup>−</sup> ions, which shifts the equilibrium to the left, increasing the concentration of ${\text{NO}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}}$ ions and decreasing the concentrations of HNO<sub>2</sub>. (d) Adding NaCl has no effect on the concentrations of the ions. (e) Adding KNO<sub>2</sub> adds ${\text{NO}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}}$ ions and shifts the equilibrium to the right, increasing the HNO<sub>2</sub> and OH<sup>−</sup> ion concentrations.

exercises.prompt:
What is the effect on the concentration of hydrofluoric acid, hydronium ion, and fluoride ion when the following are added to separate solutions of hydrofluoric acid?
(a) HCl
(b) KF
(c) NaCl
(d) KOH
(e) HF

answer.solution: Suggested approach: write HF + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> + F<sup>−</sup>. For each substance added, say which species of the equation it adds or which its ions react with, shift the equilibrium as Le Châtelier’s principle predicts, and follow the three concentrations, as the keyed answer for KNO<sub>2</sub> in the exercise before this one does.

exercises.prompt: Why is the hydronium ion concentration in a solution that is 0.10 M in HCl and 0.10 M in HCOOH determined by the concentration of HCl?

answer.solution: This is a case in which the solution contains a mixture of acids of different ionization strengths. In solution, the HCO<sub>2</sub>H exists primarily as HCO<sub>2</sub>H molecules because the ionization of the weak acid is suppressed by the strong acid. Therefore, the HCO<sub>2</sub>H contributes a negligible amount of hydronium ions to the solution. The stronger acid, HCl, is the dominant producer of hydronium ions because it is completely ionized. In such a solution, the stronger acid determines the concentration of hydronium ions, and the ionization of the weaker acid is fixed by the [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] produced by the stronger acid.

exercises.prompt:
From the equilibrium concentrations given, calculate Ka for each of the weak acids and Kb for each of the weak bases.
(a) NH3: [OH−] = 3.1 × 10−3 M;
$[{\text{NH}}_{4}{}^{\text{+}}]$ = 3.1 × 10−3 M;
[NH3] = 0.533 M;
(b) HNO2: $[{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{\text{+}}]$ = 0.011 M;
$[{\text{NO}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}}]$ = 0.0438 M;
[HNO2] = 1.07 M;
(c) (CH3)3N: [(CH3)3N] = 0.25 M;
[(CH3)3NH+] = 4.3 × 10−3 M;
[OH−] = 3.7 × 10−3 M;
(d) ${\text{NH}}_{4}{}^{\text{+}}:$ $[{\text{NH}}_{4}{}^{\text{+}}]$ = 0.100 M;
[NH3] = 7.5 × 10−6 M;
[H3O+] = 7.5 × 10−6 M
Determine Ka for hydrogen sulfate ion, ${\text{HSO}}_{4}{}^{\text{-}}.$ In a 0.10-M solution the acid is 29% ionized.

answer.hint: 29% ionized makes [H3O+] = [SO42−] = 0.029 M and leaves 0.071 M of HSO4−.

exercises.prompt:
Calculate the ionization constant for each of the following acids or bases from the ionization constant of its conjugate base or conjugate acid:
(a) HTe− (as a base)
(b) ${({\text{CH}}_{3})}_{3}{\text{NH}}^{\text{+}}$
(c) ${\text{HAsO}}_{4}{}^{2–}$ (as a base)
(d) ${\text{HO}}_{2}{}^{\text{-}}$ (as a base)
(e) ${\text{C}}_{6}{\text{H}}_{5}{\text{NH}}_{3}{}^{\text{+}}$
(f) ${\text{HSO}}_{3}{}^{\text{-}}$ (as a base)

parts.hint: Kb = Kw/Ka with Ka for HTe− from H2Te in Appendix H.
Kb = Kw/Ka, with the second ionization constant of arsenic acid.
Use Kw and the Kb of phenylamine (aniline) in Appendix I.
Kb = Kw/Ka, with the first ionization constant of sulfurous acid.

exercises.prompt:
Calculate the concentration of all solute species in each of the following solutions of acids or bases. Assume that the ionization of water can be neglected, and show that the change in the initial concentrations can be neglected.
(a) 0.0092 M HClO, a weak acid
(b) 0.0784 M C6H5NH2, a weak base
(c) 0.0810 M HCN, a weak acid
(d) 0.11 M (CH3)3N, a weak base
(e) 0.120 M $\text{Fe}{({\text{H}}_{2}\text{O})}_{6}{}^{2+}$ a weak acid, Ka = 1.6 × 10−7

answer.solution:
(a) $\frac{[{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{\text{+}}][{\text{ClO}}^{\text{-}}]}{[\text{HClO}]}\;=\;\frac{(x)(x)}{(0.0092-x)}\;\approx \;\frac{(x)(x)}{0.0092}\;=2.9\;\times \;{10}^{-8}$
Solving for x gives 1.63 × 10−5 M. This value is less than 5% of 0.0092, so the assumption that it can be neglected is valid. Thus, the concentrations of solute species at equilibrium are:
[H3O+] = [ClO–] = 1.6 × 10−5 M
[HClO–] = 0.0092 M
[OH−] = 6.1 × 10−10 M;
(b) $\frac{[{\text{C}}_{6}{\text{H}}_{5}{\text{NH}}_{3}{}^{\text{+}}][{\text{OH}}^{\text{-}}]}{[{\text{C}}_{6}{\text{H}}_{5}{\text{NH}}_{2}]}\;=\;\frac{(x)(x)}{(0.0784-x)}\;\approx \;\frac{(x)(x)}{0.0784}\;=4.3\;\times \;{10}^{-10}$
Solving for x gives 5.81 × 10−6 M. This value is less than 5% of 0.0784, so the assumption that it can be neglected is valid. Thus, the concentrations of solute species at equilibrium are:
$[{\text{C}}_{6}\text{H}5{\text{NH}}_{3}{}^{\text{+}}]$ = [OH−] = 5.8 × 10−6 M
[C6H5NH2] = 0.0784 M
[H3O+] = 1.7× 10−9 M;
(c) $\frac{[{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{\text{+}}][{\text{CN}}^{\text{-}}]}{[\text{HCN}]}\;=\;\frac{(x)(x)}{(0.0810-x)}\;\approx \;\frac{(x)(x)}{0.0810}\;=4.9\;\times \;{10}^{-10}$
Solving for x gives 6.30 × 10−6 M. This value is less than 5% of 0.0810, so the assumption that it can be neglected is valid. Thus, the concentrations of solute species at equilibrium are:
[H3O+] = [CN−] = 6.3 × 10−6 M
[HCN] = 0.0810 M
[OH−] = 1.6 × 10−9 M;
(d) $\frac{[{({\text{CH}}_{3})}_{3}{\text{NH}}^{\text{+}}][{\text{OH}}^{\text{-}}]}{[{({\text{CH}}_{3})}_{3}\text{N}]}\;=\;\frac{(x)(x)}{(0.11-x)}\;\approx \;\frac{(x)(x)}{0.11}\;=6.3\;\times \;{10}^{-5}$
Solving for x gives 2.63 × 10−3 M. This value is less than 5% of 0.11, so the assumption that it can be neglected is valid. Thus, the concentrations of solute species at equilibrium are:
[(CH3)3NH+] = [OH−] = 2.6 × 10−3 M
[(CH3)3N] = 0.11 M
[H3O+] = 3.8 × 10−12 M;
(e) $\frac{[\text{Fe}{({\text{H}}_{2}\text{O})}_{5}({\text{OH})}^{\text{+}}][{\text{H}}_{3}{\text{O}}^{\text{+}}]}{[\text{Fe}{({\text{H}}_{2}\text{O})}_{6}{}^{2+}]}\;=\;\frac{(x)(x)}{(0.120-x)}\;\approx \;\frac{(x)(x)}{0.120}\;=1.6\;\times \;{10}^{-7}$
Solving for x gives 1.39 × 10−4 M. This value is less than 5% of 0.120, so the assumption that it can be neglected is valid. Thus, the concentrations of solute species at equilibrium are:
[Fe(H2O)5(OH)+] = [H3O+] = 1.4 × 10−4 M
$[\text{Fe}{({\text{H}}_{2}\text{O})}_{6}{}^{2+}]$ = 0.120 M
[OH−] = 7.2 × 10−11 M

exercises.prompt: White vinegar is a 5.0% by mass solution of acetic acid in water. If the density of white vinegar is 1.007 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, what is the pH?

answer.hint: One liter of vinegar has a mass of 1007 g, 5.0% of it acetic acid; convert to molarity, then solve x2/(c − x) = 1.8 × 10−5 for x = [H3O+].

The pH of a solution of household ammonia, a 0.950 M solution of NH3, is 11.612. Determine Kb for NH3 from these data.

answer.hint: pOH = 14.00 − 11.612 gives [OH−] = [NH4+]; subtract it from 0.950 M for [NH3].
